Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Vibe-coded AD enumeration report artifacts written by PowerShell (AD_*.csv + AD_Report.html) · [LLM] s5cmd.exe staged in C:\ProgramData used for bulk exfiltration on Windows · [LLM] SharpShares.exe network share enumeration post-AD-recon
Vibe-coded AD enumeration report artifacts written by PowerShell (AD_*.csv + AD_Report.html) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the file-drop signature of the Huntress 'Untitled1.ps1' AI-generated AD enumeration script: a burst of fixed-named CSV/TXT/HTML exports (AD_Users.csv, AD_Trusts.csv, AD_Report.html, etc.) written together into a C:\AD_Reports_<datetime> staging folder by powershell.exe. Article-specific because it keys on the exact output filenames and the AD_Reports_ directory prefix the script hardcodes. Rationale: Keys on the exact hardcoded output set (AD_Users.csv, AD_Trusts.csv, AD_Report.html, DNS_Subnets.txt, ...) and the C:\AD_Reports_ directory prefix documented by Huntress; the FileCount>=3 threshold suppresses any single legitimate file named AD_Report.html. Cross-checked against the Huntress primary write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1482 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A GPO/inventory PowerShell job that legitimately exports Get-ADUser data to a CSV named AD_Users.csv (rare with the exact multi-file set)
  • Identity governance tooling (a homegrown AD audit script) writing several AD_*.csv reports on a schedule
  • A pentest/red-team engagement running the same public AD-audit script
  • Backup of a prior AD_Reports_ folder being copied, re-triggering file-create events
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("C:\\ProgramData\\Untitled1.ps1","AD_Reports_") or FileCount >= 5
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm powershell.exe launched a .ps1 (look for C:\ProgramData\Untitled1.ps1) and check whether the parent chain traces to an RDP session. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the powershell process, and disable/reset the account that ran it; preserve the C:\AD_Reports_<datetime> folder and .zip for IR. 3) Hunt: on the same host and account, look for s5cmd.exe / SharpShares.exe execution within ~30 min and for the AD_Reports_*.zip archive being read/exfiltrated.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("AD_Users.csv","AD_Computers.csv","AD_Groups.csv","AD_OUs.csv","AD_Subnets.csv","AD_Trusts.csv","AD_Users_With_Email.csv","AD_Simple_Users.csv","AD_Report.html","DNS_Subnets.txt")
   or FolderPath startswith @"C:\AD_Reports_"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| summarize FileNames=make_set(FileName), FileCount=dcount(FileName), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ScriptCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath
| where FileCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("AD_Users.csv","AD_Computers.csv","AD_Groups.csv","AD_OUs.csv","AD_Subnets.csv","AD_Trusts.csv","AD_Users_With_Email.csv","AD_Simple_Users.csv","AD_Report.html","DNS_Subnets.txt")
   or TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\AD_Reports_"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| summarize FileNames=make_set(TargetFileName), FileCount=dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath
| where FileCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Vibe-Coded AD Enumeration Report Artifacts Written
id: 6b2f0a1e-9c7d-4f3a-8e21-4a1c2d5b7e90
description: Detects the fixed output filenames produced by the Huntress AI-generated Untitled1.ps1 Active Directory enumeration script.
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1087.002
  - attack.t1482
  - attack.t1018
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_files:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\AD_Users.csv'
      - '\AD_Computers.csv'
      - '\AD_Groups.csv'
      - '\AD_OUs.csv'
      - '\AD_Subnets.csv'
      - '\AD_Trusts.csv'
      - '\AD_Users_With_Email.csv'
      - '\AD_Simple_Users.csv'
      - '\AD_Report.html'
      - '\DNS_Subnets.txt'
  selection_dir:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\AD_Reports_'
  condition: selection_files or selection_dir
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\AD_Report.html OR *\\AD_Users.csv OR *\\AD_Trusts.csv OR *\\AD_Computers.csv OR *\\AD_Groups.csv OR *\\AD_Users_With_Email.csv) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\AD_Reports_* OR *\\ad_reports_*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(AD_Users|AD_Computers|AD_Groups|AD_OUs|AD_Subnets|AD_Trusts|AD_Users_With_Email|AD_Simple_Users)\.csv$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\AD_Report\.html$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\DNS_Subnets\.txt$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\AD_Reports_/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctFiles))
| DistinctFiles >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_names dc(Filesystem.file_name) as file_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("AD_Users.csv","AD_Computers.csv","AD_Groups.csv","AD_OUs.csv","AD_Subnets.csv","AD_Trusts.csv","AD_Users_With_Email.csv","AD_Simple_Users.csv","AD_Report.html","DNS_Subnets.txt") OR Filesystem.file_path="C:\\AD_Reports_*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_count>=3 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_names dc(Filesystem.file_name) as file_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("AD_Users.csv","AD_Computers.csv","AD_Groups.csv","AD_OUs.csv","AD_Subnets.csv","AD_Trusts.csv","AD_Users_With_Email.csv","AD_Simple_Users.csv","AD_Report.html","DNS_Subnets.txt") OR Filesystem.file_path="C:\\AD_Reports_*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_count>=3 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
s5cmd.exe staged in C:\ProgramData used for bulk exfiltration on Windows AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of s5cmd (an Amazon S3 bulk file-transfer tool) on a domain-joined Windows endpoint, which the actor dropped to C:\ProgramData\s5cmd.exe and used ~30 minutes after AD enumeration to bulk-exfiltrate the AD_Reports archive. s5cmd is essentially never legitimately present on Windows servers, making the binary name plus the ProgramData path a high-fidelity signal. Rationale: s5cmd.exe is a purpose-built S3 bulk-transfer binary with no legitimate footprint on a domain-joined Windows Server; Huntress observed it dropped to C:\ProgramData\s5cmd.exe and used to exfiltrate the archived AD data. Matching on filename + OriginalFileName + cmdline catches renamed copies. Corroborated by the Huntress primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vibe-coded-malware-ai-powershell/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DevOps/data engineer legitimately using s5cmd for S3 sync from a build/jump server
  • Backup or media-asset pipelines that ship data to S3 via s5cmd
  • A security team's own exfil-simulation / DLP test using s5cmd
  • A container/CI runner image that bundles s5cmd being executed interactively
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\" or IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessCommandLine for the target endpoint/bucket and source path (expect the C:\AD_Reports_<datetime>.zip archive) and confirm whether it ran in an RDP session (IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block/kill the process, and if a destination bucket/endpoint is present add it to egress deny lists; rotate any credentials reachable from the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for the preceding AD_*.csv exports and SharpShares.exe, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the s5cmd process making public outbound connections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "s5cmd.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "s5cmd.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "s5cmd"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\s5cmd.exe" or CommandLine has "s5cmd"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: s5cmd S3 Transfer Tool Execution on Windows Endpoint
id: 3a9d1c44-2b6e-4d70-9f18-5c7e0a2b1d33
description: Detects execution of s5cmd, an Amazon S3 bulk-transfer utility abused for exfiltration after AD enumeration (Huntress vibe-coded intrusion).
references:

SharpShares.exe network share enumeration post-AD-recon AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of SharpShares, a C#-based network-share enumeration tool the actor deployed alongside s5cmd to locate user-accessible data repositories after mapping AD. Named-binary detection with high fidelity because SharpShares is an offensive-security tool with no benign business use. Rationale: SharpShares is a well-known .NET share-enumeration offensive tool (no legitimate use); the article names it explicitly as deployed alongside s5cmd. Filename + OriginalFileName + cmdline match handles renamed binaries. Corroborated by the Huntress primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/08/huntress-uncovers-vibe-coded-malware-used-to-map-active-directory-environments/
ATT&CKT1135 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An authorized red-team/pentest engagement running SharpShares
  • A defender validating share-permission hygiene with the same public tool
  • A security researcher testing SharpShares in a lab image that is also managed by the EDR
  • A file renamed to SharpShares.exe by an internal audit script (rare; OriginalFileName clause still fires)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture ProcessCommandLine (SharpShares flags like /threads /ldap /outfile reveal scope and output path) and identify the initiating account and RDP context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the process, and lock the executing account; collect any share-inventory output file. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host/account for the AD_*.csv exports (preceding) and s5cmd.exe exfiltration (following), and review which enumerated shares were subsequently accessed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "SharpShares.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "SharpShares.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "SharpShares"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\SharpShares.exe" or CommandLine has "SharpShares"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharpShares Network Share Enumeration Tool Execution
id: c1e7b920-8f43-4a2d-b6c0-7d2e9f1a4b55
description: Detects execution of SharpShares, an offensive network-share enumeration utility used in the Huntress vibe-coded AD intrusion.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

RDP interactive logon followed by tool execution staged in C:\ProgramData AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a successful RemoteInteractive (RDP) logon with a valid account against subsequent process execution from C:\ProgramData\ (or a command line referencing it, e.g. powershell -File C:\ProgramData\Untitled1.ps1) on the same host within 2 hours. Mirrors the article's initial-access-then-stage pattern where the actor RDP'd in with pre-compromised creds and ran tooling out of ProgramData. Rationale: Ties the article's two grounding facts (RDP with pre-compromised creds + tools staged/run from C:\ProgramData, incl. Untitled1.ps1) into one correlation rather than alerting on either alone; the 2h window and RemoteInteractive logon type cut the noise of ProgramData writes by installers. Corroborated by Huntress. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1078 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin RDPing in and running a legitimate installer/agent that executes from C:\ProgramData (e.g. vendor updaters)
  • RMM/patch tooling launching helper binaries out of ProgramData during a remote support session
  • Software deployment where an MSI extracts and runs a stub from C:\ProgramData shortly after an admin logon
  • A jump-box where interactive RDP and ProgramData-based tooling are the norm
Suppression filter
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","s5cmd.exe","SharpShares.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "Untitled1.ps1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RdpUser/RemoteIP are expected for that server and inspect the executed FileName/CommandLine — flag powershell.exe running C:\ProgramData\Untitled1.ps1, s5cmd.exe, or SharpShares.exe. 2) Contain: if the process is offensive tooling or the source IP is unexpected, isolate the host and disable the account, then reset the pre-compromised credential set. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts the same RemoteIP/account RDP'd to, and search for AD_*.csv exports and AD_Reports_*.zip archives org-wide.
let Window = 2h;
let RdpLogons = DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess" and LogonType == "RemoteInteractive"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project LogonTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, RdpUser = AccountName, RemoteIP;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\ProgramData\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner RdpLogons on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (LogonTime .. LogonTime + Window)
| project LogonTime, ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, RdpUser, RemoteIP, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
let Window = 2h;
let RdpLogons = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 10
    | where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
    | project LogonTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, RdpUser = TargetUserName, RdpSourceIP = IpAddress;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName startswith @"C:\ProgramData\" or CommandLine has @"C:\ProgramData\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| join kind=inner RdpLogons on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (LogonTime .. LogonTime + Window)
| project LogonTime, ExecTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, RdpUser, RdpSourceIP, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(*\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\programdata\\*) OR @CommandLine:(*\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\programdata\\*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\ProgramData\\/i OR CommandLine=/\\ProgramData\\/i)
| join(query={#event_simpleName=UserLogon LogonType=10}, field=aid, include=[UserName, RemoteAddressIP4])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Inbound Cisco Smart Install (TCP/4786) from external hosts — CVE-2018-0171 exploitation AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated Cisco Smart Install (SMI) connections on TCP/4786 arriving from non-internal source IPs, the exact vector FSB Center 16 / Static Tundra uses to exploit CVE-2018-0171 and dump running/startup configs. SMI should never be reachable from the internet, so external-sourced 4786 traffic is high-fidelity. Rationale: TCP/4786 (Smart Install) is the concrete CVE-2018-0171 exploitation port named in the FBI/CISA advisory and Talos report; external-sourced 4786 has essentially no legitimate use, giving a low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/static-tundra/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/cve-2018-0171-static-tundra-smart-install-detection-guide.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Cisco DNA Center / SMI director legitimately provisioning switches (should be internal source, hence the private-IP exclusion)
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) probing 4786 from a scanning subnet
  • Red-team engagement testing SMI exposure
  • Firewall NAT hairpin re-presenting an internal SMI director as an external-looking IP
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a Cisco IOS/IOS-XE device and whether SMI (`vstack`) is actually enabled; check firewall logs for a follow-up TFTP (UDP/69) transfer from the same device to an external host. 2) Contain: block TCP/4786 at the edge, run `no vstack` on the device, and rotate SNMP community strings and device credentials that may be in the dumped config. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across all edge devices, review device running-config for unexpected `snmp-server` / ACL changes, and search for SYNful Knock implant indicators on the affected hardware.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 4786
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 4786
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP) by SourceIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, CommunicationDirection
| order by Hits desc

TFTP config-file exfiltration from network devices to external servers (UDP/69) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound TFTP (UDP/69) from internal network-device or host address space to a public IP — the exfil channel Static Tundra uses after enabling the local TFTP server on a compromised Cisco device to pull the startup/running configuration to actor-controlled servers. Rationale: The advisory and Talos report specify TFTP as the exact protocol used to copy device configuration files to actor-controlled servers; external-destined UDP/69 from the infra segment is a rare, high-signal exfil indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/static-tundra/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820
ATT&CKT1602.002 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate network backup/config archive tool (RANCID, SolarWinds NCM) using TFTP to an on-prem collector that resolves to a public-looking IP
  • PXE / IP-phone firmware provisioning over TFTP to a cloud-hosted server
  • Vendor TAC troubleshooting session uploading a config via TFTP
  • Managed-service-provider config pull from an external management network
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source device and whether it is a managed network appliance; correlate with any preceding TCP/4786 (SMI) hit and check the device for an unexpectedly-enabled TFTP server. 2) Contain: block outbound UDP/69 at the edge, disable the on-device TFTP server, and treat the exfiltrated config as compromised — rotate all credentials and SNMP strings in it. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device that has sent UDP/69 to the same external IP, review config-change history and syslog on those devices, and check for persistence (SYNful Knock, rogue local accounts, modified ACLs).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 69
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 69
| where isnotempty(DestinationIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), BytesOut = sum(SentBytes), Hits = count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by BytesOut desc

External SNMP sweep (UDP/161) probing many internal devices with default/weak community strings AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single external source hitting UDP/161 across many internal destinations — the SNMP-scanning behaviour FSB Center 16 uses to locate routers accepting default/weak community strings (e.g. 'public'/'anonymous' read-write) before issuing config-copy commands. Threshold on distinct targets separates a scan from normal monitoring. Rationale: The advisory explicitly describes internet-wide SNMP scanning for default/weak community strings as the primary Center 16 discovery method; the distinct-target threshold turns raw UDP/161 into a scan-shaped signal. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/static-tundra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/fbi-warns-russian-fsb-linked-hackers.html
ATT&CKT1602.001 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized external monitoring/NMS (e.g. cloud-hosted PRTG/LibreNMS) polling many devices over SNMP
  • Approved ASM/vulnerability scanner enumerating SNMP exposure from a cloud scan node
  • ISP or MSP network-management platform polling CPE
  • Shodan/Censys-style internet research scanning (benign but noisy)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic([""]))   // populate with sanctioned external NMS/scanner IPs to suppress known monitors
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source IP is a sanctioned monitoring/scanning service; if not, check whether any probed device responded (2-way UDP/161) and whether it uses a default community string. 2) Contain: block SNMP at the edge, migrate to SNMPv3 with authPriv, and replace 'public'/'private'/'anonymous' community strings on all responding devices. 3) Hunt: for any device that answered, look for a follow-on SMI (TCP/4786) or TFTP (UDP/69) event from the same actor infrastructure and review the device config for tamper.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 161
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Targets = dcount(RemoteIP), Hits = count(), SampleProc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName
| where Targets >= 25   // 25 = one host SNMP-touching many external devices = sweep, not routine polling
| order by Targets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 161
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), Hits = count() by SourceIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor
| where Targets >= 25   // 25 = external source probing many internal devices = scan vs. legit monitor
| order by Targets desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.dest) as target_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=161 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where target_count >= 25 AND NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - target_count
Endpoint or device beaconing to Static Tundra (FSB Center 16) actor IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects internal network devices or hosts initiating sustained low-volume outbound sessions on network-management protocols (TFTP/SNMP) to newly-seen external IPs — the actor-controlled-server callback pattern Static Tundra uses to retrieve dumped configs and maintain access. Baselines against 30-day history so only first-seen external destinations surface. Rationale: Ties the article's 'exfiltrate to actor-controlled servers' claim to a first-seen-external-destination baseline on the exact management ports (TFTP/SNMP) named, avoiding invented IP IOCs the article never provided. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/static-tundra/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820
ATT&CKT1071 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New cloud-hosted NMS/monitoring endpoint added to the environment (first-seen but legitimate)
  • SNMP-trap forwarding (UDP/162) to a newly-provisioned SIEM/collector
  • Vendor firmware/config server contacted for the first time during a maintenance window
  • Network migration re-pointing devices at a new management IP block
Suppression filter
| where DestinationIP !in (dynamic([""]))   // populate with approved NMS/collector IPs to suppress sanctioned management egress
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the external destination is not a sanctioned monitoring/collector endpoint; enrich the IP against threat intel and check whether the same source previously received an inbound SMI (4786) hit. 2) Contain: block the external IP, restrict management-plane egress to approved collectors via ACL, and rotate any credentials/community strings on the source device. 3) Hunt: sweep all infrastructure devices for connections to the same IP or ASN, inspect device configs for tamper and persistence (SYNful Knock), and validate SNMPv3/no-SMI hardening was applied.

Entra OAuth device-code flow sign-in (black-queen / saroula01 AiTM technique) AIExploitation High
Hunts successful Microsoft 365 sign-ins that completed via the OAuth device authorization grant, the exact flow saroula01's black-queen fork abuses: the victim clears MFA on genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin while the attacker's backend polls the token endpoint and redeems the access/refresh token. Legitimate device-code use is rare and confined to a handful of apps, so a device-code redemption to Office/Exchange/Graph by a normal user is a high-fidelity token-theft signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's central saroula01/black-queen technique (OAuth device code flow). Multiple external sources (Volexity, Silverfort, Microsoft) confirm SigninLogs.AuthenticationProtocol=="deviceCode" as the canonical detection field; Defender AADSignInEventsBeta does not expose this flow marker, so defender_kql is intentionally empty (Sentinel SigninLogs is the correct home). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lexfo.fr/opendir-to-phishing-operator.html • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Azure CLI / Az PowerShell 'az login --use-device-code' by developers
  • Microsoft Teams Rooms / Surface Hub and other input-constrained device enrolments
  • IoT / conference-room device provisioning
  • New employee onboarding using device-code join on a shared kiosk
  • Legit smartTV/console Microsoft account sign-ins by remote staff
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Authentication Broker","Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Visual Studio Code","Windows Sign In")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged CorrelationId in SigninLogs and check whether the recipient app/resource (Exchange, Graph, Office) matches any legitimate device-code use for that user; compare the sign-in IP/geo/UserAgent to the user's baseline. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-MFA; if confirmed, disable the account. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same IP/UserAgent across other users, review AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for token auto-refresh from that IP, and audit new mailbox rules / OAuth app consents created after the sign-in.
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol =~ "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0                                   // successful token redemption
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Authentication Broker","Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Visual Studio Code","Windows Sign In")
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

M365 sign-in sourced from known codemado/mail-argenta AiTM proxy IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Direct IOC match on Entra sign-ins whose source IP is one of the four Evilginx/SimpleHelp AiTM proxy hosts Lexfo cataloged. With Evilginx acting as a reverse proxy, Microsoft records the sign-in from the proxy's IP, so any successful auth from these addresses is the AiTM relay in action. Rationale: Uses the four AiTM proxy IPs from the article's pre-extracted IOC set; 185.163.204.7 (Budapest Evilginx+SimpleHelp host) is independently confirmed by gbhackers and Lexfo's own blog. Sign-in-from-proxy-IP is the cleanest AiTM fingerprint; Falcon leg catches any endpoint beaconing to the same hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lexfo.fr/opendir-to-phishing-operator.html • https://gbhackers.com/evilginx-operators-stealing-microsoft-365/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/open-directory-exposes-evilginx/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating the IOC in a sandbox / threat-emulation range
  • Threat-intel researcher browsing the infrastructure from a corporate egress
  • Shared NAT/VPN egress coincidentally reusing a recycled hosting IP after takedown
  • IP re-allocated to a benign tenant by the Hungarian hoster post-rotation
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm the sign-in succeeded (ResultType==0); if so treat the account as compromised regardless of MFA, since AiTM relays a full authenticated session. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens and reset credentials for the affected UPN, block the four IPs at the identity-provider and egress layers, and add them to the CA named-locations blocklist. 3) Hunt: search 30 days of SigninLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for the same UPNs from other IPs (token replay), and review OAuth grants, mailbox forwarding rules, and inbox rules created since first hit.

Single M365 account: token auto-refresh fan-out across many IPs (stolen-session keepalive) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Lexfo-described pattern of the same corporate mailbox being re-authenticated non-interactively many times from multiple distinct IPs as operators refresh stolen tokens before they age out (article notes tokens set to autoRefresh, some refreshed up to 25 times). A single user with a high non-interactive success count spread over several source IPs in one hour is a strong session-hijack indicator. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific forensic detail (97 live tokens set to autoRefresh, some refreshed 25 times; same accounts captured from different IPs as tokens aged out). Threshold-and-window correlation, so Sigma/Datadog/Falcon are intentionally omitted (aggregation lives at rule level; identity refresh telemetry is not in FDR). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lexfo.fr/opendir-to-phishing-operator.html • https://cyberpress.org/device-code-phishing-bypasses-mfa/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile users roaming across carrier/Wi-Fi IPs generating frequent silent token refreshes
  • Split-tunnel VPN or CGNAT churn presenting many source IPs per user
  • Heavy Outlook/Teams/OneDrive multi-client usage (phone+laptop+web) refreshing tokens
  • Service-like accounts polling Graph from load-balanced egress
  • Conditional Access token-lifetime policies that force frequent silent re-auth
Suppression filter
| where not (DistinctIPs <= 4 and array_length(set_intersect(IPs, IPs)) > 0)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the IP set for the flagged UPN — legitimate roaming clusters within one ASN/geo, whereas hijack shows an operator IP (often a hosting ASN, e.g. the Budapest range) interleaved with the victim's normal IP. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens and sessions for the account, reset credentials, and require phishing-resistant re-MFA; enable CAE-capable Conditional Access to invalidate stolen sessions faster. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the anomalous IP against UC2's proxy IOCs and the device-code detection, and check whether the same IP refreshes tokens for other users.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0                                    // successful token issuance
| where IsInteractive == false                            // token auto-refresh leg
| summarize Refreshes=count(), DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,25), Apps=make_set(Application,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctIPs >= 3 and Refreshes >= 15              // 15 = keepalive floor; article cites up to 25 refreshes per token
| order by Refreshes desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0                                   // successful non-interactive token issuance
| summarize Refreshes=count(), DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,25), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctIPs >= 3 and Refreshes >= 15              // 15 = keepalive floor; article cites up to 25 refreshes per token
| order by Refreshes desc

Contact with codemado/saroula01 phishing lure domains (picis.net, romnor.ca) AIDelivery High
IOC match on DNS/web/email contact with the three AiTM phishing domains tied to the operators, including the picis.net host that kept provisioning fresh subdomains through May 2026. Any resolution or HTTP request to these domains (or their wildcard subdomains) flags a user who reached the Evilginx/device-code lure. Rationale: Uses the three phishing domains from the article/IOC set (picis.net and romnor.ca named explicitly as the two operator domains; queeenspropertyservices.ca from the extracted IOCs). Wildcard coverage catches picis.net's continually-rotating subdomains noted in the timeline. Corroborated by Lexfo and THN. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lexfo.fr/opendir-to-phishing-operator.html • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually visiting the domain during triage/investigation
  • Secure email gateway / URL-detonation sandbox resolving the link
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling auto-resolving IOCs
  • Domain later parked/sinkholed and resolving to a benign holding page
  • Passive DNS or scanning appliance in the environment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal src/host and whether the contact was a click (UrlClickEvents ClickAllowed/ClickedThrough) versus automated resolution; pull the full URL for device-code vs Evilginx path indicators. 2) Contain: block the domains and wildcards at DNS/proxy/mail gateway, and if a real user clicked, pre-emptively revoke that user's M365 sessions and force re-MFA. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/user to UC1 (device-code sign-in), UC2 (proxy-IP sign-in), and UC3 (token-refresh fan-out) within a few minutes of the contact to confirm session capture.
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca"]);
union isfuzzy=true
 (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where UrlDomain in~ (PhishDomains) | extend Source="EmailUrlInfo", Pivot=Url, Host="", Account=""),
 (UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (PhishDomains) | extend Source="UrlClickEvents", Pivot=Url, Host="", Account=AccountUpn),
 (DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any (PhishDomains) | extend Source="DeviceNetworkEvents", Pivot=RemoteUrl, Host=DeviceName, Account=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
| project Timestamp, Source, Pivot, Host, Account
| order by Timestamp desc
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca"]);
union isfuzzy=true
 (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (PhishDomains) | extend Source="DnsEvents", Pivot=Name, Actor=ClientIP),
 (ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any (PhishDomains) | extend Source="ImWebSession", Pivot=Url, Actor=SrcIpAddr),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL has_any (PhishDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (PhishDomains) | extend Source="CommonSecurityLog", Pivot=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Actor=SourceIP)
| project TimeGenerated, Source, Pivot, Actor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args Installation High
schtasks.exe /create or Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler EventID 4698 with LOLBin actions.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64","\Users\Public","\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64",
                              "\Users\Public", "\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Micros Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Micros
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("evilginx2.exe", "xeox-agent_x64.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("evilginx2.exe", "xeox-agent_x64.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceProcessEvents

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where (FileName in~ ("evilginx2.exe", "xeox-agent_x64.exe"))

iCagenda 'icagenda-batch/1.0' scanner + web shell fetch (CVE-2026-48939) AIDelivery High
Hunts the automated iCagenda exploitation chain: the attacker's scanner user-agent 'icagenda-batch/1.0' and/or any HTTP request to a .php file under the component's attachment path 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/'. That folder only ever holds event attachments, so a PHP request there is a planted web shell being fetched. Rationale: Uses two article-verified, near-zero-FP IOCs: the attacker-built scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' and the fixed attachment path 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' — a PHP GET there is the planted shell being retrieved. Both confirmed by mySites.guru's advisory and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/ • https://www.securityweek.com/organizations-warned-of-exploited-joomla-extension-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or bug-bounty researcher replaying the public CVE-2026-48939 PoC against your own site
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) crawling the attachments path and generating 404s
  • Legitimate iCagenda event attachment coincidentally named with a .php substring in the query string but returning 404
  • Security-team validation of the patch by re-testing the submit endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending ClientIP — confirm the sequence (token GET → POST to the submit-event endpoint → GET of a .php under images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ returning 200). A 200 on the shell fetch = confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: WAF-block the source IP, take the site to maintenance or isolate the web server, and immediately delete any non-image/non-document file (especially .php) from images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/. Patch iCagenda to 4.0.8 / 3.9.15. 3) Hunt: review the Joomla user list for newly created Super User/administrator accounts, grep the webroot for recently modified PHP files, and pivot on the shell filename across other hosts and the Balbooa uploads folder.

| order by LastSeen desc

Balbooa Forms unauthenticated PHP web shell in uploads folder (CVE-2026-56291) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to a PHP file under the Balbooa Forms default upload folder 'images/baforms/uploads'. The frontend attachment upload accepted any file from an anonymous visitor with no type check, so a PHP file served from this folder is unauthenticated RCE / a live web shell. Rationale: The article gives the exact Balbooa Forms default upload path 'images/baforms/uploads' and states any PHP there is unauthenticated RCE. A .php request to a folder meant only for image/document attachments is high-fidelity; corroborated by SecurityWeek and CISA KEV. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/organizations-warned-of-exploited-joomla-extension-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/

  • Site migration/backup tooling reading files under images/baforms/ over HTTP
Suppression filter

Response runbook
1) Triage: focus on requests where Status=200 — a successful PHP response from images/baforms/uploads/ confirms an executing web shell; note the shell filename and calling IP. 2) Contain: WAF-block the source IP, isolate the web server, delete every non-image/non-document file from images/baforms/uploads/, and patch Balbooa Forms to 2.4.1. 3) Hunt: audit the Joomla user list for rogue administrator accounts, search the whole webroot for recently modified PHP files, and check the iCagenda attachments folder for the same actor (both flaws are being scanned together).

PHP web shell written into Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders AIInstallation High
Endpoint file-event detection for the payload-drop step of both CVEs: creation of a .php/.phtml/.phar file under 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' or 'images/baforms/uploads' by the web-server process. These folders should only ever contain user-uploaded images/documents — a PHP file there is a web shell. Rationale: Targets the file-write pivot both CVEs share, using the two exact folder paths from the article plus a PHP-family extension list. Excluding Joomla's benign index.php stubs keeps it near-deterministic; the web-server process in InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName confirms the write came through the vulnerable extension. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joomla or the extension writing its own protective index.php/index.html stub into the folder (excluded via filter)
  • A legitimate site restore/migration tool (Akeeba Backup) unpacking archived attachment files that include a .php
  • Developer manually placing a debug or maintenance .php in the uploads directory during troubleshooting
  • Antivirus/quarantine tooling renaming a flagged file inside the folder
Suppression filter
// Already applied inline: exclude Joomla index.php stubs
| where FileName !=~ "index.php"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file's contents and hash (SHA256) — confirm it is PHP code (eval/base64_decode/system) rather than a stub, and note InitiatingProcessFileName (should be the web/PHP process). 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, isolate the web host, and block the source IP identified from the correlated web-access log; patch iCagenda (4.0.8/3.9.15) and Balbooa Forms (2.4.1). 3) Hunt: sweep the entire webroot for other recently written PHP files, check for new Joomla administrator accounts, and pivot on the file hash and web-server process's subsequent child processes (cmd.exe/sh spawned by w3wp/php-fpm) to scope post-exploitation.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("images/icagenda/frontend/attachments", @"images\icagenda\frontend\attachments", "images/baforms/uploads", @"images\baforms\uploads")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| where FileName !=~ "index.php"   // Joomla ships empty index.php stubs in these dirs
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreated","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("images/icagenda/frontend/attachments", @"images\icagenda\frontend\attachments", "images/baforms/uploads", @"images\baforms\uploads")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","php5","phar") or TargetFilePath endswith ".php"
| where TargetFileName !=~ "index.php"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated asc

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2008-4128")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Critical

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Compromised jscrambler npm package drops binary container (dist/intro.js) AIDelivery High
Hunts the presence of the trojanized jscrambler releases by their signature artifact: a multi-megabyte dist/intro.js file that does not exist in any clean release and is actually a native-binary container disguised as JavaScript. Article-specific because legitimate jscrambler ships no intro.js at all. Rationale: Anchors on node_modules\jscrambler\dist\intro.js — a file absent from every clean release (0.1.0→8.13.0) and confirmed by StepSecurity and The Hacker News as the 7.8 MB binary container; file-size gate removes any coincidental JS named intro.js. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://safedep.io/jscrambler-npm-supply-chain-compromise/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Developer manually cloning the malicious repo for analysis in a sandbox
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample
  • Backup/restore of an old infected node_modules tree flagged as new activity
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file hash against the three known payload SHA256s and check package-lock.json for jscrambler pinned to 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any process running from the OS temp dir, and remove/quarantine node_modules; block the C2 IPs at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: sweep all CI/CD build agents and developer laptops for the same intro.js path and for temp-dir dotfile executables; treat the host as credential-compromised and force rotation of browser-stored creds and wallet extensions.

| where FileName =~ "intro.js"

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
