Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' · [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) driver load + All.exe/Allpatch2.exe · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SystemBC (socks.exe) SOCKS5 C2 to The Gentlemen infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windows event log clearing via wevtutil (Security/System) — ransomware anti-forensics · [LLM] Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic — Gentlemen pre-encryption · [LLM] Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance (The Gentlemen) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' AIInstallation High
Hunts creation/execution of any Windows scheduled task whose name or command line matches the string 'gentlemen', a naming convention Unit 42 explicitly ties to The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS deployment. This is a direct, high-fidelity string the actor bakes into its persistence/execution tasking. Rationale: Unit 42's Execution recommendation literally says to alert on any scheduled task matching 'gentlemen*'; a task name is attacker-chosen and near-zero legitimate collision, making this an alerting-grade string. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool or ticket referencing 'gentlemen' in a benign task description
  • Red-team/purple-team exercise deliberately reusing the actor's task name for detection validation
  • A vendor product or hostname coincidentally containing the token 'gentlemen'
  • Internal threat-hunt scripts that grep for 'gentlemen' and echo it into a task command line
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe","taskschd.msc") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\Users\\Public\\","\\ProgramData\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task action/XML and the parent process of schtasks.exe; confirm the task points at an unsigned or temp-path binary and note the creating account. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, disable and delete the task, and suspend the creating account pending review. 3) Hunt: sweep the domain for the same task name via GPO (The Gentlemen abuse GPOs for domain-wide deploy), and pivot on the referenced binary hash across all endpoints.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
    | where AdditionalFields has "gentlemen"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=tostring(AdditionalFields), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
  )
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName has "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (EventID in (4698, 4699, 4702) and EventData has "gentlemen")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Scheduled Task Named gentlemen
id: 8f2a1c6e-7b4d-4e11-9c2a-3f5b8d1e77a1
description: Detects creation or execution of a scheduled task matching the string 'gentlemen', tied to The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) ransomware.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'gentlemen'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.security ((@EventID:4688 @CommandLine:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)) OR (@EventID:4698 @EventData:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(schtasks|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/gentlemen/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe OR Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe OR Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
GentleKiller BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) driver load + All.exe/Allpatch2.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts The Gentlemen's GentleKiller EDR-killer chain: the vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys driver being loaded/dropped (exploiting CVE-2025-7771) and execution of the framework loaders All.exe / Allpatch2.exe that abuse it to terminate 400+ security processes at kernel level. Both the driver name and loader names are corroborated by ESET and Trend Micro. Rationale: ThrottleStop.sys (CVE-2025-7771) and the loaders All.exe/Allpatch2.exe are named in the article's privesc/defense-impairment guidance and corroborated by ESET's GentleKiller writeup; a vulnerable driver of this name loading is exceptionally rare in enterprise fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the real ThrottleStop overclocking utility by an enthusiast/engineering workstation
  • Hardware benchmarking or CPU tuning software that bundles the same driver
  • Security researcher detonating a BYOVD sample in a sandbox
  • A file named all.exe from an unrelated legitimate installer (verify path/signature)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\ThrottleStop\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "TechPowerUp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the driver's signature/hash and whether ThrottleStop GUI is legitimately installed; check for immediate EDR sensor tampering or process kills right after the load. 2) Contain: isolate the host, add the driver hash to the WDAC/ASR blocklist, and force an EDR sensor health re-check. 3) Hunt: search for All.exe/Allpatch2.exe and other GentleKiller variants (HexKiller, ThrottleBlood, HavocKiller) fleet-wide and review which security processes were terminated around the load time.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "throttlestop.sys"
| extend Signal = "BYOVD driver load (ThrottleStop.sys / CVE-2025-7771)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal, ItemName = FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName in~ ("all.exe","allpatch2.exe")
    | extend Signal = "GentleKiller EDR-killer loader"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal, ItemName = FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
  )
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (EventID == 7045 and ServiceFileName has "throttlestop.sys")
    or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName has_any ("\\all.exe","\\allpatch2.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GentleKiller BYOVD ThrottleStop.sys Driver Load (CVE-2025-7771)

Windows event log clearing via wevtutil (Security/System) — ransomware anti-forensics AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the article's named defense-evasion behaviour: execution of wevtutil to clear the Security or System event logs, an anti-forensic step Unit 42 flags for behavioural alerting on Gentlemen intrusions. Anchored on wevtutil 'cl' against those two specific channels. Rationale: Unit 42's Defense Impairment recommendation explicitly calls for behavioural alerts on wevtutil clearing Security/System logs; 'wevtutil cl Security' is an attacker anti-forensic action almost never seen in legitimate admin workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing logs during troubleshooting or before imaging a host
  • Log-management/SIEM onboarding scripts that rotate local channels
  • Compliance tooling that archives-then-clears event logs
  • Golden-image build pipeline sanitising logs prior to sysprep
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","sccm.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/account and whether the clear coincided with EDR alerts, driver loads, or shadow-copy deletion on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve any forwarded/central copies of the cleared logs (they are the source of truth now). 3) Hunt: check other hosts for the same account clearing logs, and correlate the clear timestamp against ransomware staging (SystemBC, Cobalt Strike) activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (EventID == 1102)
    or (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName has "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log") and CommandLine has_any ("Security","System"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic — Gentlemen pre-encryption AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the article's Impact recommendation: deletion of Volume Shadow Copies via vssadmin, wmic, or PowerShell WMI, the standard Gentlemen pre-encryption step to inhibit recovery. Anchored on the specific 'delete shadows' / 'shadowcopy delete' / Win32_Shadowcopy invocations. Rationale: Unit 42's Impact recommendation names vssadmin and wmic shadow-copy deletion directly; the 'delete shadows' / 'shadowcopy delete' invocations are near-exclusively ransomware and legit shadow lifecycle rarely runs in interactive user context. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Commvault backup jobs that clean up pre-snapshot shadow copies
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting VSS storage exhaustion with 'vssadmin delete shadows /all'
  • Disk-imaging or migration tooling resetting shadow storage
  • Windows Server maintenance scripts pruning old restore points
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","vsnapvss.exe","beremote.exe","cvd.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName != "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process (services.exe vs an unsigned binary/ransomware) and whether backup software owns the account; a non-backup, non-SYSTEM parent is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately — shadow deletion is typically minutes before encryption — and freeze backups/snapshots at the storage layer. 3) Hunt: check for concurrent wevtutil clears, GentleKiller driver loads, and mass file renames; validate offline backup integrity before any restore.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows")
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy","Remove-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy","Win32_Shadowcopy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName has "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete shadows")
    or (NewProcessName has "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Win32_Shadowcopy")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via vssadmin or wmic
id: a4f6c1b2-9d38-4e7a-b512-77c0e9a1d233
description: Detects deletion of Volume Shadow Copies, a pre-encryption Inhibit System Recovery step used by The Gentlemen ransomware.
references:

logsource:
  category: process_creation

detection:
  vssadmin:
    Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'delete'

  wmic:
    Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'shadowcopy'
      - 'delete'
  condition: vssadmin or wmic
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\vssadmin.exe OR *\VSSADMIN.EXE) @CommandLine:(*delete*shadows* OR *Delete*Shadows*)) OR (@Image:(*\wmic.exe OR *\WMIC.EXE) @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\vssadmin\.exe$/i CommandLine=/delete\s+shadows/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\wmic\.exe$/i CommandLine=/shadowcopy/i CommandLine=/delete/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/Win32_Shadowcopy/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=vssadmin.exe AND Processes.process="*delete*shadows*") OR (Processes.process_name=wmic.exe AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR ((Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Win32_Shadowcopy*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=vssadmin.exe AND Processes.process="*delete*shadows*") OR (Processes.process_name=wmic.exe AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR ((Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*Win32_Shadowcopy*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
SystemBC (socks.exe) SOCKS5 C2 to The Gentlemen infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to The Gentlemen's SystemBC C2 IPs (notably 45.86.230.112, an externally-confirmed SystemBC SOCKS5 node) and/or the socks.exe proxy implant reaching public IPs. SystemBC provides the actor's RC4-encrypted SOCKS5 tunnel used before encryptor deployment. Rationale: 45.86.230.112 is corroborated by Check Point/THN as a SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 node for The Gentlemen; the article lists it alongside 193.233.202.17 and 77.110.122.137, and socks.exe is SystemBC's canonical binary name. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/systembc-c2-server-reveals-1570-victims.html • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/
ATT&CKT1090 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal host renamed socks.exe for a legitimate proxy utility (verify path/signature)
  • Threat-intel platform or sinkhole deliberately beaconing the IPs for validation
  • IP re-allocation after takedown to a benign hosting tenant (re-verify IOC freshness)
  • Security scanner probing the C2 IPs from a SOC jump box
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process owning the connection (socks.exe / rundll32.exe) and confirm the remote IP is still attributed to SystemBC; capture the parent chain. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the perimeter, isolate the beaconing host, and kill/quarantine the implant binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the implant hash and look for the Cobalt Strike fallback (rundll32.exe egress) and Advanced IP Scanner recon that typically precedes encryption.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "socks.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.86.230.112","193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen SystemBC C2 Network Connection

Advanced IP Scanner internal reconnaissance (The Gentlemen) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the network mapping tool Unit 42 and Trend Micro observe The Gentlemen using for internal recon before lateral movement. Anchored on the binary name and product metadata so renamed copies are still caught. Rationale: Unit 42's Discovery recommendation names Advanced IP Scanner explicitly; matching both the binary name and embedded product metadata catches renamed copies, though legitimate IT use makes it hunting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/IT staff legitimately mapping a subnet during troubleshooting
  • MSP onboarding scans of a new client network
  • Network inventory or asset-discovery routines run by IT ops
  • A pentest engagement using the same free tool
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","rundll32.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the running user/host is an authorised IT asset and whether the scan ran from a temp/Downloads path with an unusual parent. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and review what subnets/hosts were enumerated. 3) Hunt: correlate the scan with subsequent SMB lateral movement, GentleKiller driver loads, or SystemBC C2 on the same or scanned hosts to distinguish recon-before-ransomware from benign IT use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-7771", "CVE-2023-27532", "CVE-2024-37085")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2025-7771", "CVE-2023-27532", "CVE-2024-37085")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TSDProxy: Internal proxy auth token forwarded to backend services enables management API escalation

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API · [LLM] Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint
TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process invoking the tsdproxy management API on 127.0.0.1:8080 while injecting the leaked internal secret header x-tsdproxy-auth-token together with an attacker-controlled x-tsdproxy-id. These header names are unique to tsdproxy (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8) so their presence in a command line is a direct signature of the token-replay privilege-escalation exploit. Rationale: Keys on the two header names (x-tsdproxy-auth-token, x-tsdproxy-id) shown in the article's repro curl, paired with the fixed 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 management endpoint — all strings are unique to this vuln so an in-cmdline match is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked GitLab advisory mirror and CVEReports. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A maintainer or pentester validating the GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 fix by running the exact repro curl
  • Automated security-scanning tooling replaying the header to confirm the instance is patched
  • Internal red-team exercise reproducing the token-replay chain
  • A developer's shell-history / documentation snippet echoing the curl example that gets captured by process telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy") and ProcessCommandLine !has "scanner" and DeviceName !in~ ("pentest-lab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the initiating process/user; confirm the source process is a proxied backend (curl/wget/python/node/php) rather than the tsdproxy binary itself, and whether x-tsdproxy-id was set to a non-empty attacker value. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, rotate the tsdproxy internal token by restarting the service, and set identityHeaders: false pending upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review management API access logs (/api/v1/proxies, proxy restart/pause, webhook triggers) around the event, and check other backends sharing the tsdproxy host/network namespace for the same header string.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TSDProxy Internal Auth Token Replay to Management API
id: a1f4c2e0-8b3d-4c6a-9e21-7f0d5b3a9c11
description: Detects a process injecting the tsdproxy internal secret header (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) with a spoofed x-tsdproxy-id against the 127.0.0.1:8080 management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8).

  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/

  - attack.t1068

      - 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token'
      - 'x-tsdproxy-id'
  target:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '127.0.0.1:8080'
      - 'localhost:8080'
      - '/api/v1/'
  condition: token and target
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-auth-token* OR @process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-id*) (@process.command_line:*127.0.0.1:8080* OR @process.command_line:*localhost:8080* OR @process.command_line:*\/api\/v1\/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/x-tsdproxy-(auth-token|id)/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the tsdproxy management API path /api/v1/ on port 8080 arriving over loopback — the exact surface an attacker hits after stealing the forwarded token to enumerate proxies or issue admin operations (restart/pause/webhook). Because legitimate management access is Tailscale-fronted, loopback /api/v1 traffic bearing the tsdproxy identity headers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the concrete management endpoint (/api/v1/proxies) and port 8080 named in the article's repro, scoped to loopback where the token-replay must originate; captures the network-layer view the process-cmdline UC can miss when the attacker replays from a compiled backend rather than curl. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate tsdproxy self-calls to its own management API over loopback during normal operation
  • Local health-check or monitoring probe hitting /api/v1 on 8080
  • Admin using an SSH tunnel to reach the management UI, appearing as a loopback source
  • Container orchestration readiness/liveness probes against the management port
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication has_any ("curl","python","wget","go-http-client","node") or RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client user-agent (RequestClientApplication) and method — a curl/python UA or a POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/v1 from loopback is high-suspicion vs the tsdproxy service's own calls. 2) Contain: block external reachability to the management port, rotate the internal token via service restart, and disable identityHeaders. 3) Hunt: correlate with process telemetry (UC token-replay cmdline) on the same host and review whether proxy configs were enumerated or services restarted/paused via the API.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationPort == 8080
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/"
| where SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or DestinationIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog service:tsdproxy ("/api/v1/proxies" OR "/api/v1/")
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest_port=8080 (Web.url="*/api/v1/proxies*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/*") (Web.src="127.0.0.1" OR Web.src="::1") by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest_port=8080 (Web.url="*/api/v1/proxies*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/*") (Web.src="127.0.0.1" OR Web.src="::1") by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080 AIExploitation Low
Surfaces a proxied backend process (curl/wget/python/node/php/shell) opening a connection to 127.0.0.1:8080 — the precondition the advisory calls out for token replay (backend must reach the management port on loopback). Pairs the leaked-token capture with the network reachability that turns it into management-API takeover. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's stated precondition ('attack requires the backend to reach 127.0.0.1:8080'); scoping to interpreter/CLI processes hitting loopback:8080 catches the reachability step even when the token itself isn't in a logged command line. Higher FP by nature, so hunting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backend app legitimately configured to call the management API over loopback (e.g., an admin dashboard on the same host)
  • Local monitoring/health-check scripts probing 8080
  • Another unrelated service also listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 (common dev port)
  • CI/CD or debug tooling on the host issuing loopback requests to 8080
  • Interpreter processes performing normal intra-host service calls unrelated to tsdproxy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("x-tsdproxy-auth-token","x-tsdproxy-id","/api/v1/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm 8080 on the host is the tsdproxy management listener (not an unrelated dev service) and inspect the initiating process command line for the tsdproxy identity headers. 2) Contain: if the process is an untrusted/compromised backend, isolate the container, rotate the token via service restart, and set identityHeaders: false. 3) Hunt: pivot to process-cmdline telemetry for x-tsdproxy-auth-token on the same aid/host and review management API logs for enumeration or state-changing calls.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 8080
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","php","ruby","perl","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan Electron renderer spawns OS shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS to RCE, CVE-2026-50551) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-50551 where a stored XSS in an attribute-view cell runs in the SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration:true) and calls require('child_process') to spawn native commands. A note-taking app parenting cmd/powershell/wscript/etc. is the high-fidelity signal that the XSS payload fired. Rationale: Parent binary siyuan.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin is the article's exact RCE mechanism (Electron nodeIntegration:true -> require('child_process')); corroborating write-ups confirm proof payloads like require('child_process').exec('calc') hence calc.exe is included. A note app has no legitimate reason to parent these binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-39846/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — confirm InitiatingProcessCommandLine shows the SiYuan renderer (--type=renderer) and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for downloaders (certutil/curl/bitsadmin) or discovery. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the SiYuan process tree, and quarantine any second-stage file the child wrote/downloaded; identify the SiYuan workspace and pull data/storage/av/*.json for the payload. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device syncing the same workspace/account (the payload propagates via sync) and run UC2 across them; verify all SiYuan installs are >=3.7.0.

SiYuan attribute-view JSON planted/synced by non-SiYuan process (CVE-2026-50551 payload staging) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the persistence/delivery stage of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious attribute-view cell lives in data/storage/av/<avID>.json and reaches victims via workspace sync or a direct file drop (the PoC drops poc.json). Flags writes to that path by any process other than the SiYuan binaries — i.e. a cloud-sync client or manual plant staging the stored-XSS payload before a panel open fires it. Rationale: The article pins the payload store to data/storage/av/<avID>.json and states the file rides normal sync; the PoC drops poc.json directly. Writers other than siyuan.exe/siyuan-kernel.exe (a Dropbox/OneDrive/Syncthing client or a scripted drop) staging that exact path are the delivery vector. Note: EDR file telemetry carries no file content, so this pivots on path+writer, not the </textarea><img onerror> string. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-56mp-4f3v-fgj2
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1080
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party sync client (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, Syncthing, Resilio) propagating benign attribute-view edits made on another device
  • Backup/AV software touching the workspace and re-writing the JSON with its own process context
  • User manually copying/restoring a workspace folder with Explorer (explorer.exe) or a copy tool
  • Workspace stored on a network/synced share where a remote host is the effective writer
  • SiYuan portable build run from a path where the binary name differs (rename)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","googledrivefs.exe","syncthing.exe","resilio sync.exe","explorer.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the flagged data/storage/av/*.json and grep its cell values for HTML breakout patterns (</textarea>, <img, onerror=, onclick=, javascript:) — content isn't in EDR telemetry so you must read the file. Confirm the writing process (sync client vs unexpected tool). 2) Contain: if malicious content is present, remove/neutralize the row, block the SiYuan panel open on that record, and quarantine the file across sync peers; snapshot for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 on every host that syncs this workspace to see if a panel open already spawned a shell; confirm all SiYuan clients are upgraded to >=3.7.0 which replaces string HTML insertion with safe DOM APIs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName) and ActingProcessName !has "siyuan"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"

FileBrowser proxy-auth bypass (CVE-2026-54089): direct inbound to app process bypassing reverse proxy AIDelivery Medium
Hunts direct network connections accepted by the FileBrowser (`filebrowser`) process from public/non-RFC1918 sources. In a correct proxy-auth deployment (auth.method=proxy) ALL traffic is fronted by nginx/Traefik/Caddy on loopback; any direct client reaching the app port can forge the X-Remote-User header for full admin takeover, so a direct inbound connection is the pre-condition for exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete `filebrowser` binary and the article's stated proxy-auth trust model (all traffic should arrive via loopback/proxy). A public-sourced inbound connection is the necessary pre-condition for the header-forgery bypass; cross-checked against GLAD advisory and FileBrowser Quantum proxy-auth docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monitoring/uptime probes (Uptime-Kuma, Prometheus blackbox_exporter) hitting the exposed port from a monitoring host
  • Administrator accessing FileBrowser by IP:port directly for debugging, bypassing the proxy
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/OpenVAS) connecting to the port
  • Public load-balancer or Kubernetes kubelet liveness/health checks against the container port
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP — is it a known monitoring/LB/scanner asset or an unexpected external client? Check LocalPort matches the FileBrowser publish port and whether the host is meant to be proxy-fronted only. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, firewall the FileBrowser port to the reverse-proxy IP only (or rebind the container to 127.0.0.1), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any minted admin tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same SourceIP in web/proxy access logs for POST /api/login followed by /api/settings or /api/users (UC2/UC3), and review the FileBrowser user store for accounts created out-of-band.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"        // the FileBrowser Go binary
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"                          // proxy-auth setups should only see loopback/proxy
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8085                            // FileBrowser published port (article PoC -p 8085:80)
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","accept","") or isempty(DeviceAction)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) and SourceIP != "127.0.0.1"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: forged X-Remote-User / X-Original-User header on /api/login AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to FileBrowser's /api/login endpoint that carry a proxy-auth identity header (X-Remote-User / X-Original-User / Remote-User) sourced from the client rather than injected internally by the trusted proxy. FileBrowser unconditionally trusts this header to mint a JWT for any username (including admin) with no password check, so a client-supplied header on the login path is direct exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable endpoint (/api/login) and the trusted header name (X-Remote-User, per proxy.go and FileBrowser Quantum docs) plus the documented aliases. A client-set proxy-auth header on the login path is the literal exploit primitive; header capture at the proxy is the only place this value is visible (not in Defender/FDR endpoint tables). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowserquantum.com/en/docs/configuration/authentication/proxy/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The trusted reverse proxy's own hop legitimately injecting X-Remote-User (if the access log records post-injection headers on the loopback request)
  • Security scanners or authorized pentesters testing specifically for CVE-2026-54089
  • Internal tooling misconfigured to forward the identity header
  • Automated SSO integration test suites exercising the proxy-auth flow
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request SourceIP is NOT the reverse-proxy address — a client-supplied X-Remote-User from any other IP is exploitation. Note the username value in the header (admin = full takeover). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, and rotate the JWT signing key to revoke minted tokens; review the impacted account's actions. 3) Hunt: correlate the same SourceIP to subsequent /api/settings and /api/users calls (UC3), and search the user database for accounts auto-created from unknown usernames.
Syslog

| where ProcessName in~ ("nginx","caddy","traefik","apache2","httpd")
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/login"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("X-Remote-User","X-Original-User","Remote-User")   // requires log_format that records the request header
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser CVE-2026-54089: admin-endpoint access immediately after /api/login from same client (privilege jump) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a FileBrowser /api/login request with admin-only API calls (/api/settings, /api/users, /api/resources with write/delete) from the same source IP within a 2-minute window. The proxy-auth bypass lets an unauthenticated client obtain an admin JWT in one request; a session that logs in and immediately performs admin actions with no legitimate elevation is the post-exploitation signature. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete admin endpoints (/api/settings, /api/users) reachable only by an admin JWT, correlated to the /api/login mint within a tight window. The temporal login->admin-action shape captures the credential-less privilege jump the CVE enables without needing header visibility, so it works on plain access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1548 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator logging in then editing settings/users as part of normal workflow
  • Automation or IaC scripts that authenticate then provision users via the API
  • Backup or inventory tooling enumerating /api/resources shortly after auth
  • The reverse proxy's own health probe hitting /api/settings after a synthetic login
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the SourceIP is the reverse proxy (expected) or a direct external client (suspicious). Confirm the login used proxy-auth and identify the username/permission set that performed the admin action. 2) Contain: if the client is untrusted, block the IP, rebind FileBrowser to loopback, rotate the JWT signing key, and audit any settings/user changes made in the window. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP to UC1 (direct inbound) and UC2 (forged header), and diff the FileBrowser user store and settings against the last known-good backup for unauthorized changes.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let Window = 2m;
let Logins = CommonSecurityLog
